title: Which length is longest and which is shortest?
description: Seven groups of lengths in tenths and hundredths are compared by writing each group in the same small part and counting. Keeko doubts the comparison and thinks a hundredth makes a length longer.
teaching_notes: One idea: to compare lengths, write them all in the same small part and compare the counts. Watch for students who think hundredths are bigger because one hundred is a bigger number than ten.

video_script.why: The child can write a length in tenths and hundredths and now compares lengths by writing each group in the same small part.
video_script.substitution: Write every length in a group as a count of the same small part, then the biggest count is the longest and the smallest count is the shortest.
video_script.anchor: Seven groups of lengths in tenths and hundredths, shown as bars on a unit scale
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks 3/100 is the longest of 3/10, 3/100 and 33/100 because 100 is bigger than 10, but a hundredth is a smaller part, so 3/100 is the shortest.
video_script.payoff_line: In every group, change all lengths to the same small part and compare the counts

final_answer.value: Group 1: 33/100 longest, 3/100 shortest; Group 2: 3 1/10 longest, 1 3/10 shortest; Group 3: 54/100 longest, 4/10 shortest; Group 4: 3 6/10 6/100 longest, 3 6/100 shortest; Group 5: 1 8/100 longest, 2/100 shortest; Group 6: 7 5/10 longest, 7 3/10 5/100 shortest; Group 7: 6 5/10 15/100 longest, 5 7/100 shortest
final_answer.spoken: in each group the length with the most small parts is the longest and the length with the fewest small parts is the shortest

hold_back: Group 1: 33/100 longest, 3/100 shortest; Group 2: 3 1/10 longest, 1 3/10 shortest; Group 3: 54/100 longest, 4/10 shortest; Group 4: 3 6/10 6/100 longest, 3 6/100 shortest; Group 5: 1 8/100 longest, 2/100 shortest; Group 6: 7 5/10 longest, 7 3/10 5/100 shortest; Group 7: 6 5/10 15/100 longest, 5 7/100 shortest
never_show: 3/100 marked as the longest of group 1
maths_rules: Slip: a hundredth is a smaller part than a tenth, so a bigger denominator does not make a longer length.
video_script.design: One idea: write all lengths in a group as counts of the same small part, then compare counts. Assumes the child can change tenths to hundredths. Wrong idea: a bigger denominator means a longer length. The seven groups stay on the board and only some counts are spoken.
open_questions: Group 5: the worklist reads 8/100, 2/100, 9/100, 1 8/100 (shortest 2/100), but the book question reads 8/10 2/100, 9/100, 1 8/100 and the book answer key gives the shortest as 9/100. The video follows the worklist; check the group 5 question against the book.
